issues.evidence: probe p_file_blocks_dir; A/organizer.py:48 dest_dir.mkdir outside try -> 'FileExistsError: [Errno 17] File exists: txt', rc=1; in --watch the process died and later.jpg was never organized
issues.summary: If a top-level file has the same name as an extension folder (for example a file named 'txt' next to foo.txt), mkdir raises an error nothing catches, so --once stops partway and the --watch process dies.
Watch mode moves files as soon as it sees them and does not check whether they are still being written.

issues.evidence: A/organizer.py:83 --log default 'organizer.log' is relative to the CWD, so running from another directory writes the log there, not in the target
issues.summary: Where the log ends up depends on the directory the program is run from, not on the target directory.
Files with .tmp, .part, .crdownload or .download extensions are left unmoved and nothing is logged, which the task did not ask for.

blinding_guess.why: A ships a test suite whose tests map one-to-one onto the stated requirements (stdlib-only, single file, mode exclusivity, log not moved), which suggests a spec-driven process; B looks like a pragmatic hand-written script.

notes: Probes ran on Python 3.9.6 with cwd set to the target directory for both sides, so A's CWD-relative log lands in the target. Each side failed one different probe: A crashes on a file/folder name clash (it also kills --watch, confirmed manually), and B deliberately skips temp-download extensions. B waits for two identical scans before moving a file in watch mode, which is safer but adds about one interval of delay. Bandit flagged only A's test subprocess use (low); neither organizer.py has security findings. pytest is not installed, so A's tests were run with unittest.
